title: Politics live: Coalition dials up pressure on PM over $6m grant to golf club; Trump administration warns Australia after social media algorithm reform
text:
The Coalition has dialled up the pressure with frontbencher Tony Pasin asking the prime minister to explain the $6m grant given to a golf club in his electorate, a club which he’s an honorary member of.
Before the PM can begin answering, Labor MP Ash Ambihaipahar is kicked out of the chamber for interjecting too much.
Anthony Albanese gets to a shouting volume pretty quickly, saying (as he did this morning) that it was one of three grants to his electorate and that the money was to stop sewage running from the course into the local Cooks River.
He also claims he didn’t know that he’d received the honorary membership.
I’m asked about honorary membership. In 2012, I’d been advised that I got honorary membership, someone made a decision. I don’t have a card. I don’t go to the club.
Frontbencher Aaron Violi then tries to table documents in the house “clearly showing the prime minister’s longstanding relationship with the Marrickville golf club including being a location where he injured himself and developed a black eye and broken rib” but the government blocks the attempt.
As that happens, Labor MP Alison Byrnes is also ejected from the chamber!
Coalition ‘led by the nose’ by One Nation on tobacco excise: Butler
Liberal MP Mary Aldred is up next and asks the prime minister if he’ll cut the tobacco excise – yes or no – pointing out that he’s refused to rule out doing so when recently asked.
The health minister, Mark Butler, takes the question instead (which attracts jeers from the opposition).
Butler claims under the previous government the excise was raised 215%, but no money was spent on law enforcement or public health campaigns.
He uses similar lines to Anthony Albanese this morning that enforcement and border control are the focus, and then decides to take a stab at the Coalition.
Of course we are open to other sensible ideas about how we can fight organised crime while not prejudicing our most important public health campaign. But this is the problem I have with the announcements that One Nation first made and then, sure enough led by the nose, the Coalition followed.
Labor considering calls for nationally consistent definition of affordable housing
Will the government back a nationally consistent definition of affordable housing, so it can be delivered and made available to nurses, teachers and other key workers asks independent MP, Nicolette Boele. She says more than 12,000 Australians have signed a petition calling for a national approach.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers (answering questions for Clare O’Neil today, who’s away) acknowledges that the states and territories do all have different definitions.
Chalmers says the government is aware and looking at the issue.
The Housing Australia Future Fund requires rents for affordable tenancies to be set at a 25% discount to market rents. That’s how the Haff goes about this but it’s different across different states and programs … [O’Neil] has asked Treasury to do work on affordable housing definitions including looking at the different definitions and frameworks that currently operate across Australia and to see what our options are for more consistency. We do think that’s an important objective.
‘I don’t play golf’: Albanese dismisses questions about honorary membership
And we’re back to the $6m Marrickville golf club grant with deputy Nationals leader, Darren Chester, asking if the prime minister should update his register of interests with the honorary membership because a full membership costs $1,100 a year.
Anthony Albanese repeats that he was just told that “apparently” he received the honorary membership in 2012 unbeknownst to him.
He then jokes that he doesn’t play golf, and he’ll leave the sport to the deputy prime minister, Richard Marles. This is kind of funny because Marles has previously faced some sticky questions about whether he ever used taxpayer-funded VIP RAAF flights to travel to golf courses.
Albanese says he doesn’t even go to the golf course, except walking his dog through it and once attending a dog’s birthday there.
The fact is that in 2012, they said ‘You’re an honorary member’. I don’t have a card, I never got anything, I don’t use the facilities, I don’t do anything whatsoever for it.
Systematic fraud claims in home battery scheme ‘a lie’, says Bowen
Nationals MP Alison Penfold takes the baton from Tehan and asks Chris Bowen more explicitly the date he was “first made aware of allegations impacting the government’s cheaper home batteries program?
Bowen says there is a committee that regularly provides feedback on the scheme, which includes the Clean Energy Regulator.
He says the number of complaints as a proportion of installations for cheaper home batteries have halved since the program.
The opposition quickly moves in to make a point of order because they want Bowen to provide a date on when he knew about the allegations of rorts and safety issues. Speaker Milton Dick agrees and says the question was very specific.
Bowen says allegations of systemic issues are false:
I started receiving updates on the … program on 1 July 2025 and have received them regularly. Those updates have shown they the manager of Opposition’s claims of systemic fraud are not true, are a lie.
Bowen rejects opposition claims of rorting in cheaper home battery scheme
Dan Tehan is next and changes tack, he asks if the energy minister, Chris Bowen can “guarantee that all batteries installed under the government’s cheaper home batteries program have been installed safety and in compliance with technical requirements?”
He’s referring to reports in the ABC that a taxpayer funded program to encourage households to install solar batteries is being rorted. The ABC reports its received tip offs that some providers are accused of mocking up installs, using unlicensed tradies for cash jobs and leaving customers with unsafe systems.
Bowen defends the cheaper home battery scheme and says it’s one of the “world’s most rigorous schemes for compliance”.
The member refers to complaints about cheaper home batteries. I can confirm that this scheme has received 315 complaints in relation to the small scale renewable energy scheme which covers solar panel installations, battery installations and hot water installations. That is 0.04% of installations in the last 12 months.
The opposition tries to make a point of order on relevance but don’t get very far. Bowen continues:
I think every Australian of reasonableness and good faith knows that every electrical instrument and application comes with risk. A television has risks an oven has risk … That’s why you have strict regulation and enforcement and compliance.
Independent Sophie Scamps kicked out as grants questions continue
Independent MP Monique Ryan has continued the line of questioning on the $6m grant a golf club in the prime minister’s electorate received under an “invite-only” grants program that favoured Labor seats.
Ryan asks if the PM agrees that government spending should be based on merit rather than “on retaining and winning marginal seats?”
Anthony Albanese says independent Sophie Scamps sitting next to her has received critical infrastructure upgrades in her electorate and that he gets lobbied by crossbenchers at election and byelection time to fund projects.
Scamps is angry, to say the least, and starts interjecting – she’s quickly kicked out by the speaker.
Albanese says:
Those three projects are in my electorate, certainly, I am proud to say, were all worthwhile. All of them providing community benefit, or benefit for people who are most in need.

Angus Taylor starts at the dispatch box today, and asks the prime minister if he’ll “overrule his treasurer for the fourth time and scrap his cruel tax on babies”.
He’s referring to reporting in The Australian that says trusts can be exempt from the 30% tax on trusts if they fix their distributions to beneficiaries, instead of leaving them discretionary, but adding a newborn child into the trust after the cutoff date of July 2029 will revoke that exemption.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, takes the question and makes a snide remark that the Coalition takes all its questions from The Australian newspaper’s front page.
They write their questions for them every day and they’ve done it once again. I’m not taking lectures on taxes from a party who’s been sprung this week with a plan to increase income taxes on millions of Australian workers …
The changes in the budget don’t limit the way that trusts have the flexibility to add beneficiaries in the future. The option that we have put forward in the draft legislation is about providing another way for existing trusts to set out fixed interest without requiring a restructure – something they called for – but it is entirely optional for trusts to make use of this.
Kevin Rudd’s in the house today, sitting in for QT. He’ll be addressing the National Press Club tomorrow.
‘I don’t trust big tech, but I trust the Labor party a lot less’: Canavan
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, says the government should go back to the drawing board and start again on the digital duty of care bill because there isn’t “trust” in the process.
Canavan has been a vocal critic of the laws, but we understand there is an array of opinions across the party over the issue – some who are more keen to see the reforms than the Nationals leader.
One of his chief concerns is the power the communications minister will have to broaden the scope of harms that platforms have to protect adults and children from.
Speaking to reporters a little earlier, Canavan said:
I think the government needs to start again here with this because trust is very important on these issues. I don’t trust big tech, but I trust the Labor party a lot less.
Giving them these type of powers just is a non-starter, should be a completer non-starter for the Australian people, who I think like living in a democracy and like being able to speak freely, especially about their own government.
Anika Wells said earlier today that the bill won’t impact political communication or misinformation, and that those who want to read fake moon landing conspiracy theories will still be able to.
Adding some context here to Andrew Hastie calling Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce “lying cowards” a little earlier.
Hastie said yesterday Hanson and One Nation had called him a traitor after he provided evidence in court against Ben Roberts-Smith.
But Hanson told The Nightly newspaper yesterday:
I’ve never called him a traitor … I will call him a wanker.
Hastie told News24 that Hanson had posted a One Nation cartoon on her X account that called him a traitor eight times.
Victorian premier announces plan to respond to homelessness
The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, is speaking at an event at state parliament this afternoon, announcing a $24.8m six-point plan to respond to rough sleeping.
He says the plan’s centrepiece is a rollout of an online triage system that recognises homeless people by name, helps direct resources by need and helps to collate better data and insights of how many people are sleep rough each night and where they are in the state. Carroll told the event:
One of the things I’m most proud of in this plan is the very first establishing a by-names list. We must remember these people aren’t numbers. Every one of them has a name. Every one of them has a backstory, and that is the key to ending homelessness. Making sure we know these people, who they are, what’s led them to where they are, and how we help give them the pathway forward.
The plan also includes an expansion of assertive outreach workers to every area of the state, and new supported housing on the Mornington Peninsula – using money the state collects from the levy it introduced on Airbnb properties in the region. We’ve previously reported the region has largest number of homeless people in greater Melbourne.
About 140 people experiencing homelessness are known to services in the region, but experts say the real number is closer to 300.
The minister for homelessness, Nick Staikos, says:
One of the first visits I made as minister for housing was the Mornington Peninsula. It has the largest number of rough sleepers outside of Melbourne CBD, and it has a very, very high number of women sleeping rough. It is also a place with a lot of properties listed on short stay platforms, and so we will fund supported housing on the Mornington Peninsula out of the short stay levy.
Liberal frontbencher and SAS veteran Andrew Hastie has called Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce “lying cowards”, after he claimed a One Nation cartoon referred to him as a traitor for providing evidence in court against Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation case against Nine newspapers.
In the cartoon, posted to Hanson’s X account, the Hastie character refers to himself as a “stupid traitor” after referencing his evidence for Roberts-Smith. Other characters in the animated video refer to him as a traitor also.
It’s a further escalation after Hastie in a letter to supporters, promised a costly fight against One Nation yesterday.
I deployed twice on combat operations to Afghanistan. I left my wife at home, knowing that I might not return. And then to be called a traitor by One Nation … well, they’ve picked a fight with the wrong veteran.
Speaking to News24 today, Hastie said the cartoon, which Hanson posted on her X account, used the term “traitor” many times.
I would say that Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce are lying cowards, and I’ll say it again, so there’s no ambiguity. They are lying cowards … when you start calling me a traitor to my own country, then we have a big, big problem.
Are they saying the same thing of the other 20 SAS combat veterans who gave evidence under oath in the federal court? Are they also traitors to their country?
And so I’m calling on Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce to own this cartoon. And if they own it, step out into the house or outside the house, I don’t really care, use parliamentary privilege or don’t, and explain why I and other veterans, and indeed serving members of the ADF, who think war crimes are wrong, are traitors to their country.
In response, Hanson claimed to The Nightly newspaper:
I’ve never called him a traitor … I will call him a wanker.
Domestic violence report should ‘shame governments into action’, says Steggall
The independent MP Zali Steggall says the latest report by the domestic, family and sexual violence commissioner shows “an abject failure to keep women and children safe”.
Steggall says data is unavailable for around 68% of the measures in the national plan’s outcomes framework, meaning, “we can’t manage what we don’t measure - and we can’t hold governments fully accountable when the data is missing”.
Steggall calls for increased powers for the commission to monitor government performance and compel information, launch an urgent national education plan, establish a national domestic violence offender register and establish a royal commission.
Shockingly, around 80% of police call-outs are related to domestic and family violence … Women and children don’t need more condolences and promises. They need action, accountability and a genuine national commitment to ending this crisis.
‘Pork barrelling by design’: crossbenchers push for grants process overhaul
Crossbench MPs are calling for an overhaul to strengthen the commonwealth grants system after it was revealed the government used most of a $560m invite-only fund to support infrastructure projects in safe, marginal or target Labor seats.
The MPs want mandatory and enforceable standards for grants administration, transparency over funding decisions and a non-government chaired parliamentary committee to ensure compliance of grants under commonwealth rules.
Helen Haines, who was a key campaigner for the national anti-corruption commission, claimed in a statement:
Sports rorts was pork barrelling by deception, this is pork barrelling by design … My private member’s legislation would serve as a safeguard and won’t stop governments investing in local infrastructure. It would make sure funding is allocated fairly, transparently and in the public interest.
